newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso calls for police reform - reports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso calls for police reform - reports.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has called for a shakeup of the country's police forces after an outbreak of violence involving striking police officers, newspapers said on Wednesday.
"What we have seen in the last few days cannot take place in a country with a degree of democracy and progress," Cardoso was quoted as saying on Tuesday in Sao Paulo where he is on holiday.

"The time has come for (the government) to discuss profoundly how to have a more integrated police force which is able to serve without scaring the public and with rigorous discipline," the president told daily Gazeta Mercantil.

Earlier Tuesday, striking police exchanged gunfire with on-duty officers in the northeastern city of Fortaleza, Ceara state. Six people were injured in the gunbattle, including Ceara's military police commander. The army was put on standby to deal with any new trouble.

The clash was the third time that protests by police over meagre pay has boiled over into armed conflict. In Minas Gerais state, a police officer was shot and killed during a demonstration in June. Earlier this month striking police officers and army soldiers in Alagaos state traded shots.

The dispute prompted calls for a thorough reform of Brazil's police system which is a three-tier system including the military and civil police forces, both of which are run by state governments, and the federal police.

The future of the military police, which despite its name is not part of the armed forces, has been questioned after a string of rights abuses. Human rights groups said the institution was created as a tool of repression by Brazil's 1964-85 military dictatorship and has failed to adapt to democracy.

National Human Rights Secretary Jose Gregori, a close friend of the president, is drawing proposals for a merger of the military and civil polices, a move which would make Brazil's police more answerable to civilian rule, officials said.
